title: Yesterday

notes: **This past tense is for completed events**, usually with a clear time frame: *ayer* (yesterday), *el sábado*, *la semana pasada*, *en 2020*. Spanish has another past tense for habits and background, but that's A2 — this one first.
**-er and -ir verbs share one set of endings.** *Comí, comiste, comió…* and *salí, saliste, salió…* follow exactly the same pattern. So there are only two lists to learn, not three.

**The stress moves to the last syllable, and the accent mark decides the meaning.** *Hablo* = I speak (now); *habló* = he spoke (yesterday). One small mark separates both the person and the time — which is why accent marks are never just decoration.

**Ir and ser have exactly the same past forms:** *fui, fuiste, fue, fuimos, fuisteis, fueron*. *Fui a Bogor* = I went to Bogor; *fui estudiante* = I was a student. Context sorts them out, and native speakers never get confused.

**Some spellings adjust to keep the sound.** *Llegar → llegué* (not *llegé*, so the g stays hard), *buscar → busqué*, *empezar → empecé*. The change only happens in the *yo* form; the rest are normal.
**Ver loses all its accent marks:** *vi, viste, vio, vimos, visteis, vieron*. Compare other verbs, which take a mark in the *yo* and *él* forms.
**Double negatives, again.** *Yo no vi nada* is literally "I didn't see nothing" and means "I didn't see anything". You met this in Unit 10 with *nunca*; same pattern.
**¡Qué envidia!** literally "what envy!", used just like "lucky you!" in English — a light compliment, not a real complaint.

grammars.title: Past tense of regular verbs
body: Drop the -ar / -er / -ir ending and add the endings below. Note that the *nosotros* form of -ar and -ir verbs happens to be the same as the present (*hablamos*, *salimos*) — the sentence's context tells you when it happened.
after: The good news: verbs that split in the middle in the present — *querer*, *poder*, *volver*, *empezar* — mostly **become regular again** in the past for -ar and -er verbs. *Vuelvo* becomes *volví*, *empiezo* becomes *empecé*.
The bad news: a few -ir verbs still change, but only in the *él* and *ellos* forms: *dormir → durmió, durmieron*; *pedir → pidió, pidieron*. Just recognize them; don't memorize them yet.

blocks.text: A past-tense sentence is almost always introduced by one of these words. Saying one tells your listener straight away that you're telling a story, even before the verb comes out.

Note that *hace* is used for "… ago", and it goes **in front**: *hace dos días*, not *dos días hace*. You already know the same word from the weather (*hace calor*) — the uses are unrelated, a mere accident of history.
